title: Classical Athens (508/507–322 BCE)
summary: From Cleisthenes' reforms of 508/507 BCE to a Macedonian-imposed property franchise in 322 BCE, Athens was a direct democracy of adult male citizens that led a naval league, built the Parthenon and fostered drama and philosophy, while excluding women, metics and enslaved people.
card: For almost two centuries the Athenians governed themselves through an open assembly, a council of 500 chosen by lot and large citizen juries. Victory over Persia and tribute from the Delian League paid for a fleet and the Acropolis buildings, but war with Sparta, plague and the killings of the Thirty followed. Only adult men with two Athenian parents could vote; by one estimate roughly 250,000 inhabitants lived in Attica in 431 BCE, while more than 30,000 enslaved men worked in the silver mines and fleet alone.
what:
Classical Athens here means the period from the reforms of Cleisthenes in 508/507 BCE to 322 BCE, when the Macedonian regent Antipater, after Athens' defeat in the Lamian War, replaced the democracy with a franchise limited by wealth. The Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians places Cleisthenes' measures in the archonship of Isagoras: he replaced the four old tribes with ten, each drawn from city, coastal and inland districts, enlarged the council to 500 members, fifty per tribe, and made the deme the basis of citizenship. Ostracism, a vote on potsherds requiring a quorum of 6,000 votes, was first used two years after Marathon; whether Cleisthenes himself introduced it is debated.

The Athenians defeated a Persian force at Marathon in 490 BCE. Silver from the mines at Maronea paid for 100 triremes, and in 480 BCE the Persians sacked the Acropolis before that fleet fought at Salamis. In 478 BCE Athens formed the Delian League of about 140 cities; its treasury moved from Delos to Athens in 454 BCE. A law proposed by Pericles in 451/450 BCE restricted citizenship to children of two Athenian parents, and the Parthenon was built between 447 and 438 BCE, its pedimental sculpture finished in 432 BCE. At the Great Dionysia the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides competed.

The Peloponnesian War with Sparta (431–404 BCE), during which plague struck Athens from 430 BCE, ended in defeat. The Spartan-backed Thirty put at least 1,500 people to death before democracy was restored in 404/403 BCE. Socrates was tried and executed in 399 BCE; Plato founded the Academy around 387 BCE and Aristotle the Lyceum in 335/334 BCE. Philip II's victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE made Macedon supreme in Greece.

Political rights belonged only to adult male citizens; women, metics (free resident foreigners who paid an annual tax) and enslaved people had none. Demographers estimate at least 60,000 male citizens and roughly 250,000 total inhabitants in 431 BCE, while more than 30,000 enslaved men worked in the mines and navy alone; no ancient source counted women.

uncertainty.note: Start: the archon year of Isagoras ran from midsummer 508 to midsummer 507 BCE, so the reforms fall in 508 or 507 BCE (astronomical -507 or -506). End: Antipater's settlement followed the Athenian defeat at Crannon, dated by Dinsmoor to 5 September 322 BCE (Geer's Loeb note); Diodorus files these events under the archon year 323/2, a known chronological confusion. Choosing 508/507–322 BCE as bounds is a convention: it brackets the democracy rather than the art-historical 'Classical period'.

how: The democracy rested on structures Cleisthenes built after the Peisistratid tyranny ended: ten tribes that each combined demes from the city, the coast and the inland districts, a council of 500 drawn from the tribes, and registration in a deme as proof of citizenship. Over the fifth century, power passed further to ordinary citizens. Most offices were filled by lot for a single year; the assembly on the Pnyx passed laws, elected generals and decided on war and peace; juries of citizens heard cases, allotted to courts by stone machines (kleroteria), and Aristotle records juror pay as half a drachma a day. Sea power drove the rest. On Themistocles' proposal, silver from Maronea became a fleet of 100 triremes that fought at Salamis. Athens then led the Delian League, collected tribute first assessed by Aristides, moved the league treasury to Athens in 454 BCE and paid citizens and foreigners a drachma a day to build on the Acropolis. Allies that revolted, such as Thasos (465–463 BCE) and Samos (441–439 BCE), had to pull down their walls and surrender their fleets. Rivalry with Sparta led to the war of 431–404 BCE, in which Pericles' strategy brought the Athenians inside the city walls and relied on the navy. Defeat, the rule of the Thirty and Macedonian expansion followed, and in 322 BCE Antipater's 2,000-drachma property qualification removed more than 12,000 poorer men from the citizen body.
why_it_matters: Classical Athens is the best-documented early state run directly by its ordinary citizens, and its working parts survive as physical evidence: ostraka, allotment tokens, ballots and kleroteria excavated in the Agora. The same city produced the surviving canon of Greek tragedy, the Parthenon, the history of Thucydides and the schools of Plato and Aristotle; the Academy lasted until the emperor Justinian closed it in 529 CE. Its limits matter as much. The franchise excluded all women, resident foreigners and enslaved people, and the wealth that paid citizens for public service came partly from allied tribute and from slave labour, with more than 30,000 enslaved men estimated to have been needed in the silver mines and the fleet alone. Defeat in 404 BCE and the killings by the Thirty showed how quickly the system could be overturned, and the restored democracy's execution of Socrates deepened Plato's distrust of its institutions. A counterfactual shows how contingent the period was: had the Assembly shared out the Maronea silver instead of building triremes, Athens would have met the Persian invasion of 480 BCE without the fleet that fought at Salamis, and without the naval league whose tribute later funded the Acropolis buildings. The end came by force, not decay: in 322 BCE a Macedonian property qualification stripped more than 12,000 poorer Athenians of their citizenship, leaving about 9,000 men in control of the city.

perspectives.holder: M. H. Hansen, largely accepted by B. Akrigg and reviewed by D. L. Kellogg (2021)
perspectives.account: At least 60,000 adult male citizens at the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War (431 BCE) and roughly 250,000 total inhabitants, with the population having doubled since the Persian Wars before contracting sharply from war and plague.

perspectives.holder: D. L. Kellogg (2021) in review of Akrigg
perspectives.account: Population reconstructions for Classical Athens rely predominantly on male military manpower figures, leaving women largely invisible, while categorising metics too closely with slaves flattens varied social gradations.

perspectives.holder: Thucydides and Plutarch versus Plato, as summarised by the Foundation of the Hellenic World
perspectives.account: Thucydides and Plutarch present Pericles as a perceptive, persuasive leader; Plato regarded him as a demagogue.

perspectives.holder: Scholars interpreting Pericles' citizenship law of 451/450 BCE
perspectives.account: Some read the law as a restriction on the number sharing citizen privileges; others as protection for direct democracy against unchecked growth of the citizen body. The Constitution of the Athenians links it to the large number of citizens.

perspectives.holder: Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians versus some modern scholars
perspectives.account: The Constitution counts ostracism among Cleisthenes' new laws; the Foundation of the Hellenic World notes that his authorship is only argued by some scholars.

numbers.label: Civic tribes created by Cleisthenes
numbers.note: Cleisthenes replaced the four ancestral tribes with ten tribes (Ath. Pol. 21.2).

numbers.note: Given as 'approximately 140' allied cities participating at the outset.

numbers.label: Total inhabitants of Attica at the start of the Peloponnesian War

numbers.label: Minimum number of enslaved men needed in the silver mines and the navy
numbers.note: Akrigg's minimum ('more than 30,000 male slaves'); excludes enslaved women and children and slaves in farming, households and workshops.

numbers.label: Property qualification for citizenship under Antipater's settlement
numbers.note: Citizenship restricted to those possessing more than two thousand drachmas (Diodorus 18.18.4).

numbers.label: Men removed from the citizen body by Antipater's 2,000-drachma qualification
numbers.note: Recorded by Diodorus (18.18.5) as 'more than twelve thousand'.

numbers.label: Men who met the property rating and kept full rights
numbers.note: Recorded by Diodorus (18.18.5) as 'about nine thousand'.

audience_note: Describes chattel slavery, including harsh conditions in the silver mines, and political killings by the Thirty; no graphic imagery.

importance.justification: The best-documented ancient direct democracy and the setting for the Parthenon, Greek tragedy and the philosophy of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, it is a reference point in curricula worldwide and must be visible from whole-planet view.
